books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Labor contract, Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47)

stimulus.text:
“…the Parties of the second Part are entitled to receive one half of all crops they may cultivate after a full and entire settlement of all claims the Party of the first Part may have against them arising under this Contract… they further agree that said portion of all crops … shall not be used or removed from the Plantation until all their indebtedness to the Party of the first Part is fully and satisfactorily settled.”

—Labor contract, Freedmen’s Bureau records for Mississippi (1865–1872)
stimulus.source_note: Labor contract from the Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47), transcribed by the National Museum of African American History and Culture. Public domain (federal record). Ellipses mark omissions inside the passage; “the Party of the first Part” is the landowner and “the Parties of the second Part” are the freed workers.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Under this contract, the freed workers’ share of the crop was paid only after

options.text: the landowner sold the cotton in New Orleans.
options.misconception: The contract says nothing about where the cotton was sold; the condition is the settlement of claims.

options.text: the workers bought the land they farmed.
options.misconception: Background: the workers owned no land; that is why they signed the contract.

options.text: the Freedmen’s Bureau approved the harvest.
options.misconception: The Bureau recorded contracts but did not approve harvests; the landowner controlled the settlement.

options.text: every claim the landowner held against them was settled.

rationales.A: The contract says nothing about where the cotton was sold; the condition is the settlement of claims.
rationales.B: Background: the workers owned no land; that is why they signed the contract.
rationales.C: The Bureau recorded contracts but did not approve harvests; the landowner controlled the settlement.
rationales.D: The contract pays the workers half the crop only “after a full and entire settlement of all claims” the landowner holds. Since the landowner kept the books and sold the supplies, the debts rarely cleared, and the workers rarely got paid in full.
rationales.general:
1. The contract’s first promise is a half share of the crop, which sounds fair.
2. But the half comes only “after a full and entire settlement of all claims.”
3. The claims are the landowner’s: supplies, tools, and food bought on credit during the year.
4. The landowner kept the books, so the settlement usually left the workers still owing.
Remember: in a contract, the condition on the payment matters more than the size of the payment.
